📚 Today you learned

Accretive vs. Dilutive Acquisitions

An acquisition is "accretive" if it adds to the acquirer's EPS/cash-flow-per-share within roughly a year or two; "dilutive" if it subtracts, usually because the acquirer paid mostly in new shares, overpaid on the multiple, or took on debt that outweighs the earnings added. SPXC's $410M all-cash FIS Water deal (closed Sept 15) is a useful real example: cash-funded (no new shares, so no per-share dilution from issuance), buying ~$105M of 2026E revenue into an existing HVAC/cooling platform — the kind of bolt-on that's usually accretive within a year if the target's margins are close to the acquirer's, since there's no share count to dig out of. Contrast that with a stock-for-stock mega-deal, where even a "strategic" acquisition can be dilutive for years if the target's earnings don't scale fast enough to outrun the extra shares outstanding. When you see "accretive to non-GAAP EPS in year one" language in a deal press release, check whether it's GAAP or non-GAAP accretive — companies routinely strip out the deal's own transaction and integration costs to get there, the same "adjusted" framing you saw with SBC back on Day 10.

Also today: Goodwill — the premium paid above a target's identifiable net assets, sitting on the balance sheet as an intangible; a large goodwill write-down later is the market's way of admitting a deal was overpaid.
